Split that stream up one particular way, and one single node ends up doing almost all the work.
Split the identical stream a different way, and that problem just doesn't happen.
Commit to an answer before I show you.
These events arrive in order, newest timestamp last, under a scheme that keeps keys sorted by value.
Where does that newest event always end up going?
answer: It's tempting to think a busy system would naturally spread new writes around to wherever there's room.
But sorting by key means there's exactly one place the highest key can live. And the newest event always has the highest key, by definition.
So it goes to one specific place, every single time, no matter how many other nodes are sitting there idle.

lines: Here's what that ordering actually buys you.
Because everything stays sorted, scanning across a range of keys means sweeping through data that's already sitting together, in order.
The cost of that convenience is exactly what you just predicted: every new write lands on whichever partition currently owns the far end of that sorted range.
Watch this happen on a real, measured run, not a hypothetical.
Ten thousand writes total, spread across ten of these ordered partitions.
Now look specifically at the five hundred most recent writes out of all of them. Every single one landed on exactly one partition.
Now run the identical stream of events through a completely different scheme.
Instead of sorting by key, hash each key first, and throw away any notion of order entirely.
Watch the same recent writes that all piled onto one partition a moment ago. They're spread across nearly every single partition now.
One more prediction before the next reveal.
A ten node cluster is using the simplest possible hashing, just taking each key's hash and dividing by the node count.
One more node joins, making it eleven. Roughly what fraction of all the existing keys now have to move to a different node?
answer: It's tempting to assume only the keys that would naturally belong to that new node have to move.
But the node count itself is baked directly into the formula for every single key's placement. Change that count, and almost every key's answer changes right along with it.
So the real number isn't small. It's nearly everything, just from adding one single node.

lines: Here's how two different, real techniques actually solve that exact problem.
Plain division-based hashing just measured remapping almost every key, the moment the node count changed.
A ring-based consistent hash, and a completely different technique called rendezvous hashing, both move only about the new node's own fair share of keys, and nothing more.
One more piece has to fit into this picture.
However you've split the data up, a request still has to find exactly which node actually owns that piece.
That routing step, whether it's handled by the client itself, by a proxy, or by whichever node happens to answer first, is a completely separate question from how many copies of that data exist.
Pull the whole topic together.
Ordering your keys buys you fast scans, at the cost of a tail that gets hammered. Hashing buys you an even spread, at the cost of that order.

Simple hashing falls apart the moment your cluster resizes. The smarter versions were built specifically so it wouldn't. And partitioning your data and replicating it are two entirely separate decisions.
One last one. A table is partitioned by range, keyed on a plain auto-incrementing order number.
A flash sale just pushed the write rate to a hundred times its normal level.
Given everything you just watched measured here: does simply adding more nodes to that cluster actually fix this?
answer: It's tempting to assume more nodes just means more capacity to absorb the extra load.
But every one of those new nodes gets its own slice of the key range. The newest order number still only ever belongs to exactly one of those slices.
So no. You'd just end up with more partitions sitting there doing nothing, while that same one partition keeps taking every single write.
